Our key finding is that any classifier operating in the data stream setting can only achieve asymptotic consistency up to a certain point, and we identify key conditions that must be met for a classifier to reach this limit. Notably, we show that the widely recognized issue of concept drift is not necessarily a barrier to consistency, and we present a new condition related to example relevance. Additionally, we reveal that the traditional problem of class imbalance can be viewed as a special case of a broader issue we term "attribute distortion." Our research also highlights the challenges facing algorithm evaluators, who must carefully consider various conditions under which a classifier's performance can be deemed consistent. To facilitate such evaluations, we propose a framework that allows them to specify the assumptions about a concept definition and stream of attributes. Our experiments demonstrate the utility of this framework in exploring the behavior of classifiers in response to distinct attribute distortion types. Our study further examines algorithm behavior when evaluators specify different attribute distortion models, and explores ways to promote consistency in classifiers handling such cases. Our work here highlights another challenge facing algorithm evaluators, who must consider multiple possible attribute distortion models along with other conditions such as class imbalance. This presents a significant challenge in terms of comprehending the behavior of classifiers in response to diverse dataset types. Our research is novel in that it provides a theoretical analysis of attribute distortion models along with existing problems such as class imbalance, revealing a greater complexity in this area. This led us to devise a new evaluation framework that enables attribute distortion models to be specified along with existing problems such as class imbalance, and perform experiments using this framework. Our results show that existing classifiers are susceptible to a wide range of attribute distortion models, and we introduce a new measure along with evaluation techniques to assist in the design of classifiers capable of handling such scenarios. This study is a significant contribution to the field, as it is the first to thoroughly examine attribute distortion models in detail. Additionally, it is unique in that it involves a collaborative effort between the paper's authors and a practitioner operating in the real-world setting of traffic flow prediction, illustrating the real-world implications of the paper's findings. The paper's results led to the development of a new measure along with evaluation techniques to assist in the design of classifiers capable of handling a wide range of attribute distortion models. The research focuses primarily on complete non-compact manifolds with a solvable Li-Yau gradient obstruction, which serves as a key tool for solving dynamic problems.  An interesting outcome arises when considering manifolds with a non-compact boundary; in these cases, ergodic measures can now be found regardless of the resolution of the Li-Yau gradient obstruction.  Additionally, this article generalizes prior findings from Gromov, Eberle, and the author regarding the existence of ergodic measures in geodesic flows. Lastly, a non-compact, flat manifold with a boundary is constructed, coupled with a geodesic flow whose associated measures are both ergodic and maximal, while also remaining independent of the manifold's boundary.  This contrasts with existing theories, as the ergodic measures in this case are not dictated by the manifold's boundary.

Natural agents often encounter difficulties due to the intricate and dynamic nature of their environment rewards. This study aims to provide a thorough examination of the complexities involved, using robotic navigation as a case study, and AI's advanced hierarchical reinforcement learning as a potential solution. Our results demonstrate the importance of exploring and learning the intrinsic rewards and goal structures of an environment to achieve efficient learning. We also confirm the potential of AI's hierarchical reinforcement learning in breaking down complex tasks into manageable parts and leveraging environmental structures. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities in goal-oriented learning and provides a pathway for the effective achievement of objectives. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel model based on cross-attention mechanisms that efficiently process video super-resolution tasks. Unlike existing self-attention models which are typically applied to images or embedded videos, our proposed framework incorporates three separate learnable embeddings: video, frame, and reconstructed image. Owing to the use of cross-attention mechanisms instead of self-attention, our model boasts significantly lower computational and memory requirements. Traditional methods for analyzing epidemic data typically focus on modeling a single rate, either infections or deaths, which are often assumed to be proportional to one another. We introduce a Bayesian model that utilizes a rate-based approach to jointly model infections and deaths, which are assumed to be related through a product rather than a proportionality constant. Investigating the behavior of massless photons within a graphene framework enables researchers to unravel the principles of quantum electrodynamics in a context-free setting. Investigating the interaction between photons and a current-carrying graphene strip allows us to explore quantum electrodynamics in a setting with no free charges, resulting in the disappearance of ultraviolet divergences. Our research demonstrates that when a photon interacts with this strip, the resulting massless photon exhibits a zero-threshold mass, a behavior reminiscent of the Higgs mechanism. However, this mass can be adjusted by changing the strip's characteristics. Moreover, when a graphene strip is paired with a gate electrode, the photon's mass displays a gate-dependent behavior, highlighting the ability to control the photon's effective mass. Lastly, our research shows that when a pair of opposite currents are driven through the strip, the photon's mass becomes tunable at the zero-temperature and zero-frequency level. These findings hold significant potential for the creation of novel quantum devices. Furthermore, the mechanism driving the photon mass, which involves the strip's electromagnetic response, could be applied to other systems, enabling the production of massless photons at will. The present study delves into the photon's effective action, using the strip's current to drive a massless photon phenomenon that is both consistent with the Dirac equation and well-defined in low-energy interactions. In contrast, the photon's mass appears to be zero below a certain cutoff frequency, meaning that the strip's response does not produce any mass up to that frequency. Fortran, MATLAB, and Haskell are evaluated based on key performance metrics related to template metadata, function calls, operator overloading, user-defined type conversions, and exception handling.  Performance tests were conducted on multiple platforms using the Hisotope++ application, with underlying code written in the listed languages to assess their performance capabilities.  By leveraging Hisotope++, we explored the properties of isotopic systems, simulating experiments to identify the most performance-effective languages.  Our analysis considers multiple criteria, weighting performance by the likelihood of need for replication in particle physics experiments.  Based on these standards, C++ and Java emerge as top contenders, with Fortran taking third place, preceded by C#.  Although Python demonstrates efficiency in scalar computations, its slow speed in matrix operations bars it from higher placement, with MATLAB performing similarly due to its extensive use of dynamic memory.  Finally, Haskell's high overhead hinders its performance, primarily in matrix operations and exception handling, despite its speed in template metadata and function calls.  Our study highlights the importance of type metadata, with languages like C++ and Java excelling in this area, and also underscores the need for efficient exception handling, with Fortran and C# showing significant strengths in this regard.  Additionally, the findings suggest that operators should be easily definable by users, with Python and MATLAB underperforming in this area, and finally, that low overhead in general operations is crucial, with Fortran, C#, Python, and MATLAB failing to meet this standard.  The results show that the most efficient languages for reproducing simulations are C++, Java, and C#, each with unique strengths that could be exploited to optimize specific tasks.  By ranking languages according to their overall performance, we provide valuable insights for computational physicists, guiding them in the choice of suitable languages to ensure high efficiency and reliability in reproducing experimental results.  The study also identifies areas for improvement in the languages evaluated and offers suggestions for enhancing performance in isotopic systems, including the potential for hybrid language usage.  The code and simulation data have been archived in public repositories for public access.

Our research will explore the underlying assumptions that guide the interplay between human and machine decision-making, highlighting their connection to broader power dynamics that shape the social fabric. Our goal is to provide actionable recommendations for courts, policymakers, and researchers to confront the inherent biases within these decision-support systems. Our investigation has also shown that the biases in these decision-support systems are not unique to Texas, but rather are reflected in the social and legal biases against Black individuals in the US as a whole. In response to these challenges, we have developed an innovative method for computing approximate probabilities of observed data under specific alternative hypotheses in the context of adaptive trials with categorical outcomes. We have utilized this package to analyze a hypothetical adaptive trial in patients with hypertension, considering two treatments and a categorical outcome measure known as the Patient Global Assessment (PGА). Our simulation revealed that adaptive trials with a targeted information criterion can provide similar levels of power as informative trials and trial designs based on Bayesian principles, while also offering increased efficiency. In contrast, trials that adapt based on a strict information criterion exhibit lower efficiency. Furthermore, we have observed a direct correlation between the degree of efficiency and the diversity of treatment effects in the groups. In light of our findings, we recommend using an intermediate adaptive trial design that balances a strict and informative approach to optimize efficiency and control variability. This method could be an attractive option for a wide range of clinical trials, especially those with categorical outcomes and an uncertain expected treatment effect. Additionally, our results can serve as a reference point for determining an optimal group diversity level. Future research will focus on expanding the SimCTT package to accommodate continuous outcomes and incorporating a method to approximate the trial's properties based on mean relative risks. In the longer term, we aim to develop a simulation tool that facilitates comparisons between various trial designs based on traditional and Bayesian principles. Additionally, it is suggested that these metrics should be informed by the goals underlying these tasks.  This is illustrated by the concept of goal-driven evaluation methods.  It is proposed that goal-driven evaluation involves the application of criteria rooted in a thorough examination of task goals during assessment.  This concept is illustrated through numerical evaluations and the analysis of a case study involving the generation of synthetic buildings.  Ultimately, it is hoped that this work will spark further discussion on the utility of evaluation methods in image synthesis and inspire the development of new, effective assessment tools.  This, in turn, is expected to contribute to the progression of image synthesis as a field. of high-resolution three-dimensional images of cells and tissues by gathering electrons scattered from a specimen. Traditional EM techniques require extensive sample preparation and involve inspecting individual specimens one by one. A novel EM technique utilizes a pellet of biological tissue containing numerous cells, collected from a routine procedure called cytosolic fractionation. This technique processes the tissue into a thin layer, ready for EM analysis, and offers the analysis of intact cells within a tissue context. An initial experiment demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique in producing high-quality images and revealed key information about the structure and organization of cells. However, this technique has practical limitations due to the presence of contaminants that hinder EM imaging, such as a thick layer of lipids that needs to be removed and certain dense structures that are difficult to process. Furthermore, the technique requires significant amounts of biological tissue, typically in the range of hundreds of milligrams to a gram, and is particularly complicated when dealing with small samples. Despite these challenges, the technique offers unique possibilities for investigating cells and tissues at the subcellular level. It has a wide range of potential applications, including the examination of immune cells within lymph nodes, the analysis of neurons and supporting cells within the brain, and studying diverse cell types within the pancreas. We discuss the technique's underlying principles, provide an in-depth examination of the processing steps, and review the current challenges and potential applications. Additionally, we present our initial results from a practice run in which we successfully obtained images of well-organized islands of pancreatic beta cells, surrounded by capillary structures resembling those found in the Islets of Langerhans at the Islet of Pancreatic Cell facility at the University of California San Francisco (UCSF). Our images demonstrate the technique's potential to investigate cells and tissues at the subcellular level with high resolution, and provide essential context for understanding the complex structure and organization of cells. Ultimately, the technique could significantly expand our knowledge of cell biology and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic tools. Furthermore, the technique may serve as a springboard for conducting in-depth immune analyses at the subcellular level, encompassing a broad scope of diverse cells, including those involved in immune reactions. By combining EM imaging with other advanced analysis techniques such as single-cell sequencing or in situ RNA sequencing, the technique could provide comprehensive and precise understanding of cells and tissues at the subcellular level, thereby facilitating the identification of specific cells, the interpretation of their shape and structure, the analysis of their cytosolic and nuclear components, the recognition of various organelles

It is through art that past generations have sought to convey their sentiments, preserving their experiences for future eras. In the present, artistic means of communication continue to evolve, adapting to technologies such as virtual and augmented reality. This has given artists a newfound arena in which to explore, express, and ultimately shape the public's perception of society. In the realm of art, VR has empowered creators to produce immersive experiences that educate, raise awareness about social issues, and inspire contemplation. This research delves into the potential of VR as a tool for social change, exemplified by its applications in art. A comprehensive database of VR art has been established, from which emerging trends and patterns can be identified. This database is based on the 2020 VR Art Survey, which analyzed the characteristics of 504 works from 231 artists, showcasing a diverse landscape of VR art. Our analysis highlights the increasing influence of VR art on social awareness, as well as its reliance on novel storytelling approaches. Furthermore, our research presents a taxonomy that categorizes VR art into styles, as well as a framework for evaluating their impact, providing a framework for critics and artists to engage with this medium. Ultimately, our study serves as a foundation for the investigation of VR art and its potential for social transformation. By analyzing this data, we can gain insight into how VR art can be utilized for positive change and inform the creative process of artists working in this field. Through our analysis, we find that VR art is most effective when it fosters a sense of shared humanity in viewers, transporting them to new and immersive environments that facilitate connection and empathy. By leveraging emerging technologies, artists can produce immersive experiences that challenge and transform society. This research demonstrates that VR art is a dynamic force for change and serves as a model for fostering meaningful transformation, offering a new approach to collective growth and evolution. By gathering statistics on VR art, we can better understand this dynamic form of art that is shaped by the technologies available at the time of creation, reflecting and influencing the societal context in which it is produced. Our study represents the first of its kind to search for binary black hole mergers using the data collected during the first two periods of joint observations between AdLIGO and Virgo, with a higher level of sensitivity than previous similar studies, covering a weight range of 20-70 solar masses, and involving a higher degree of accuracy with a probability of 0.1% or less. networks trained with gradient-based optimization has been a challenging issue for both computational scientists and theoretical researchers. A comprehensive understanding of how fundamental parameters such as learning rate, batch size, and number of iterations influence the evolution of network weights and training and testing errors is highly desirable but has not been achieved yet. This study aimed to investigate the effect of the batch size on the learning dynamics of neural networks, and we discovered that the batch size significantly impacts the observed training dynamics. Specifically, our results indicate that smaller batch sizes are associated with oscillatory behavior, leading to delayed convergence, whereas larger batch sizes typically result in smoother dynamics. Notably, our findings are contingent upon the specific batch size being larger or smaller than the number of neurons in the network. Our research provides new insights into the behavior of gradient-based optimization, and it sheds light on the origin of stagnation in deep learning, a phenomenon previously documented by Veckler et al. Our analysis also reveals that the dynamics of network weights are governed by an alternating pattern of rapid and slow updates. Furthermore, we observed that the learning rate has a profound effect on the asymmetry of the stagnation point, and we explained how this outcome is related to the eigenvalues of the network's gradient matrix. Consistent with the findings of Kottler et al, our results show that the asymmetry of the stagnation point can be used to predict whether the network will achieve optimal solutions. Additionally, our work extends the concept of stagnation points to deeper networks and reveals that the stagnation point is reached significantly faster on larger networks. Ultimately, our results shed light on the effect of batch size on the learning dynamics of neural networks, and they may inspire future research on the optimization dynamics of deep learning. But extracting named entities from large amounts of text can be very difficult and time-consuming.  Would it be possible to use an integrated system that includes both an automated method for extracting named entities and a group of human experts?  In this research, we investigate how different automated methods for extracting named entities compare to human-generated ones in the context of BERT.  We also examine how various automated methods compare to human-generated ones in the context of BERT.  Using the TREC deep web task data, we evaluate and compare the performance of several automated methods that involve extracting named entities using specific search queries.  We also combine the outputs of these methods to create a hybrid dataset of extracted named entities.  We then use this hybrid dataset in various text classification and information retrieval tasks that involve the use of named entities, and show that combining the outputs of several automated methods is better than using a single method in these tasks.  This research is the first to compare human-generated named entities to those generated using automated methods, and it provides improvements to the field of natural language processing by creating high-quality training and testing data.  It also offers an innovative solution to the named entity extraction problem, and it demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating several automated methods to produce high-quality data.  Additionally, the research shows that standard metrics for evaluating named entity extraction are not reliable, and it proposes an alternative evaluation method called the named entity accuracy metric.  This new metric evaluates the overall quality of the extracted named entities at both the document and query levels, and it rewards systems that accurately cover relevant information and penalizes systems that introduce extraneous entities.  The research also reveals some interesting patterns in the types of named entities most easily extracted using automated methods, and it explains why certain entities are more easily extracted than others.  Finally, the paper provides recommendations for improving the quality of automated named entity extraction by suggesting search queries with minimal ambiguity and optimal information content.  Based on the outcomes of the experiments, the quality of the automated named entity extraction method using the integrated system that includes both an automated method for extracting named entities and a group of human experts surpasses that of the standalone methods, demonstrating an 11.2% and 11.1% improvement in F1 score in the single-sentence and multi-sentence contexts respectively, and an 11.2% improvement in precision, precision-recall, and F1 score

A new approach to the problem of execution failure in robots is presented in this paper. It relies on the use of a planning method called planning-at-the-edge that aims to transfer the knowledge of a pre-existing task plan to a new set of goals or situations in a quick and efficient way.  This new approach is based on the connection between two concepts: the continuity of tasks and the idea of using nearby plans to achieve shared goals, which was first introduced in the field of autonomous driving and is now being applied to the robotics community.  A key aspect of this new approach is the use of a metric that measures how similar different task plans are to each other, which takes into consideration the requirements of a valid robot execution.  This metric, called the viability metric, was developed using concepts from viability theory and was tested on a variety of tasks such as stering a wheelchair, moving a lunar robot and picking up objects with a gripper.  Results have shown that execution failure recovery using this new approach occurs in a reasonable amount of time in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods.  It was also found that this method is capable of recovering task execution both quickly and accurately.  An analysis of the results has shown that the connection between task execution and planning-at-the-edge is an important area of research that deserves further investigation.  Therefore, an open-source implementation of the planning-at-the-edge method in Python is being made available for the robotics community to use.  It includes a wide range of tools and techniques that can be applied to a variety of tasks and provides users with the option to easily move from a task plan to a real-time robot execution using the modulated trajectory execution method. field of statistics has benefited significantly from advancements in computational power. As a result, statistical analysis is now inherently dependent on computational methodology. This growing reliance necessitates thorough scrutiny of the computational components that underpin statistical methods. Our work aims to initiate this evaluation by identifying potential sources of instability in statistical algorithms and developing tools to detect and mitigate these issues. Focusing on algorithms used for nonconvex optimization, we implement and test sensitive inputs called "optimal worst-case perturbations" that detect whether a method is prone to getting stuck in local optima or suboptimal solutions. Our work on optimal worst-case perturbations spans three fields: statistics, optimization, and computer science, each having distinct requirements and applications. Our research is relevant to researchers working at the intersection of computational statistics and optimization, as well as scientists using computational statistical methods, such as Bayesian inference, bootstrap resampling, and Monte Carlo integration. Additionally, the field of robustness in statistics, particularly in regression and generalized linear models, also stands to gain from this work. Our research is presented in detail in a paper titled "Robustness in Computational Statistics and Optimization: Detecting and Mitigating Worst-case Perturbations in Non-convex Algorithms" and is accompanied by a software release that allows users to calculate optimal worst-case perturbations and assess the robustness of computational statistical methods. The release includes the Python module "Robustness", designed to facilitate robustness analysis, which we demonstrate through its application to Bayesian inference and Monte Carlo integration. The module's functionality is further illustrated through our analysis of the Stochastic Gradient Descent, the EM algorithm, and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Metropolis-Hastings), highlighting the need for robust computational statistics and optimization methods. Our research aims to set a new standard for the computational components of statistical methods by prioritizing robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, as well as providing practical advice for users of statistical methods. Our work initialy appeared in ARXIV in Dec 2020, and has since been accepted in the Journal of Computational Statistics & Simulation, and is accompanied by a technical report and software release. The issue of fair representation has become a major concern, involving the creation of AI models that represent various groups, such as demographics, without bias. Existing research on fair representation focuses on avoiding data biases, but this approach has limitations. In this study, we investigate a more comprehensive concept of social justice, exploring whether machine learning models can accurately represent social justice principles in relation to tabular data. Our analysis reveals that simply removing biases in representation does not suffice; rather, representations must also be just and equitable. Additionally, we find that fair representation is feasible, not only theoretically, but also in practice, based on our evaluation of multiple social justice criteria and datasets. Importantly, we discover that applying a single standard to representations can be unjust and that individual groups may have unique representations that align with their interests. Therefore, we propose a framework for evaluating representations based on their ability to meet the needs and wants of individual groups, which ultimately guides our selection of suitable representations. Our evaluation shows that multi-group classification is a valuable tool for achieving fair representations, provided that appropriate labels and metrics are used. However, we also identify potential issues with predictive error and information overlap in multi-group classification. To address these challenges, we offer alternative labels and metrics that can facilitate just representations in the absence of accurate classification. However, the accuracy of database responses, specifically for questions asking patient-specific data, is influenced by the presence of relevant conditions in the query. To illustrate, if a doctor searches for patients with high blood pressure and heart disease, it is more crucial to have accurate answers even if some patients with high blood pressure may not have heart disease. To address this challenge, we have developed a new method that takes into account the level of required conditions for answering a database query. Our approach utilizes nonmarkovian dynamic influence models to measure the impact of conditions within a patient's record and quantify the reliance of database answers on specific conditions. By optimizing the order in which conditions are considered, we ensure maximal accuracy and can handle scenarios with multiple condition orders. To validate our method, we conducted experiments using publicly available data and found that our approach consistently outperforms static models in answering database queries accurately. Furthermore, our method successfully identified factors contributing to disorder misclassification and led to the development of an algorithm for detecting lung cancer based on information from chest X-rays. We demonstrate that a full rank orthogonal matrix always has a positive eigenvector, while eigenvectors of a unitary matrix can be either positive, negative, or bipolar. Conversely, any positive or bipolar eigenvector of a unitary matrix corresponds to a corresponding positive or bipolar eigenvector of an associated orthogonal matrix. Notably, an orthogonal matrix can be reducible along a particular axis or direction, yet remain irreducible in all others. This study examines the effects of dust aerosols on atmospheric radiation and energy balance through analyses of satellite data and climate models. By combining observations of total near-infrared reflectance and modeled estimates of dust optical properties, we calculated the mass of aerosol particles per unit area over the Earth's desert regions. This quantification allowed us to develop a statistical relationship between the mass of dust aerosols and the associated change in atmospheric energy balance, which was found to correlate positively. Additionally, we determined that an increase of 1 mg/m^2 of dust mass corresponded to an average increase of 0.09±0.10 W/m^2 in atmospheric energy balance. Furthermore, we evaluated several global climate models to assess their representations of dust aerosols and associated effects on energy balance in different regions. The models overestimated the impact of dust aerosols on energy balance in desert regions, with estimated increases more than ten times the value observed, and tended to underestimate the impact of dust aerosols in other regions. The reasons for these discrepancies are not thoroughly investigated in this study, but it is suggested that the tendency for models to overestimate the impact of dust aerosols in desert regions may be related to issues with the estimation of dust optical depth and the subsequent absorption of solar radiation, which could lead to an overestimation of energy balance impacts in desert regions. The analysis of several climate models and satellite data suggests that the incorporation of additional factors such as dust particle size distribution and variability in dust optical properties could contribute to resolving the discrepancy between observed and modeled effects of dust aerosols on energy balance. The incorporation of detailed dust aerosol representation in atmospheric energy balance models may mitigate the discrepancy between observed and modeled effects of dust aerosols in desert regions, where the discrepancy was most pronounced in this study. The analysis of satellite data and climate models provides insight into the effects of dust aerosols on energy balance in desert regions, which can help inform research into the effects of dust aerosols in other regions, such as agricultural and urban areas, and sensor applications. The study provides quantitative and qualitative connections between the mass of dust aerosols, the associated change in atmospheric energy balance, and modeled representation of dust aerosols, which can help resolve the discrepancy between observed and modeled effects of dust aerosols in desert regions. The research can help resolve a notable issue with the models of atmospheric energy balance, and contribute to the understanding of dust aerosol effects on desert climate,

The article also includes a computational tool that allows users to determine the Davenport-Schmidt invariants of cubic fields based on the Mordell-Weil group of the associated Picard variety. This comparison was possible due to recent computations of Dines-Merriman invariants and Davenport-Schmidt invariants of cubic fields made explicit. The results of this comparison indicate that the Davenport-Schmidt invariants provide a stronger classification of the cubic fields than the Dines-Merriman invariants. Furthermore, the Davenport-Schmidt invariants classify the cubic fields into 257 distinct types, whereas the Dines-Merriman invariants classify them into 216 distinct types. This poses a challenge to machine learning models, which struggle to effectively learn from the minority class due to class imbalance. To avoid conflicts and ensure safe spectrum sharing, 5G systems use dynamic spectrum sharing, activating mmWave base stations only when 6 GHz spectrum is available.  To boost mmWave base station coverage and increase the spectrum sharing efficiency, our research proposes using large-scale outdoor user equipment (UE) in crowded areas.  By strategically placing these user equipment devices near streets with high foot traffic, our analysis demonstrates significant improvements in mmWave base station coverage and the ability to share spectrum more efficiently, ultimately increasing the overall system capacity.  Analysis of the 28 GHz mmWave channel characteristics in New York City shows that large-scale outdoor UE can effectively extend the line-of-sight (LOS) coverage by 15.7% and the non-LOS coverage by 20.5%, ultimately increasing the overall coverage by 12.2%.  Furthermore, our simulation results show that strategically placing large-scale outdoor UE in high-traffic areas allows 5G mmWave spectrum sharing to activate base stations 57.1% of the time, a significant 1.5 times better performance over traditional systems.  This substantial improvement indicates that large-scale outdoor user equipment can significantly boost mmWave base station coverage and spectrum sharing efficiency, making them a promising technology for the next generation of wireless communications.  By leveraging these devices, network planners and administrators can increase the overall efficiency of 5G mmWave spectrum sharing, effectively serving a larger number of users in high-traffic environments, according to our research. In order to efficiently utilize the embedded structural information, a new method called Structural Completion of Tensors by iteratively Enhancing non-gaussian patterns (STIE) is proposed. This process involves building a database of signal strength readings at various locations within a venue and creating a database of unique signal patterns, or fingerprints. However, constructing this database proves to be labor-intensive due to the numerous readings required. This problem is particularly pronounced in venues with dense areas such as hospitals. Fortunately, we have devised an efficient system for generating WiFi signal fingerprints that doesn't necessitate extensive reading collection. Our system uses machine learning to determine the number of readings needed in each region. Initially, we conduct a quick survey to gather essential information about the signal strength environment. Based on this data, we calculate the probability of successful matching for each region and adjust the density of reading collection accordingly. By implementing this new system, the process of building a fingerprint database becomes significantly faster and less resource-intensive. Additionally, we observed an overall 0.2 meter improvement in localization accuracy compared to traditional methods. This new approach enables efficient localization in large areas with complex structures, saving time and effort. Therefore, the proposed system serves as an effective solution for generating WiFi signal fingerprints in such environments. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the relationship between the designed probabilities and localization accuracy, thereby paving the way for further innovations in this domain. Our research provides essential insights for the development of mobile device localization technologies, thereby contributing to the advancement of localization methods. The proposed system can be utilized in large areas with intricate structures such as hospitals, malls, and stadiums by tweaking the parameters. We begin by investigating whether widely employed thermal face enhancement techniques can also be explored in the opposite direction, specifically reversing them to facilitate visible to thermal conversion. We conduct an experiment at the University of Essex's facial analytics lab, gathering both thermal and visible images of 8 individuals. Our findings indicate that the reversal of conventional thermal face enhancement techniques is a feasible approach to thermal to visible face recognition, specifically when the average precision is 0.88. Research into isometric embeddings of metric spaces within the space of functions on certain sets has a long history. A significant question in this area involves determining whether any metric space has a flat, i.e., a space with only isometricly embedded metric subspaces that are either complete and have uniform distances or contain arbitrarily small distances, representation as isometric embeddings within the space of functions on certain sets. We address this question for special types of metric spaces: those that are complete and have uniform distances. Another area of research in this field involves the study of spaces with particular distance properties, such as spaces where the distance between any two points can be split equally, called ultrametric spaces, or spaces with a specific distance comparison property, called tree-metric spaces. We provide the first proof that any complete metric space with uniform distances contains a flat. Additionally, we provide separate proofs that any complete metric space with uniform distances contains both a flat and an ultrametric subspace and a tree-metric subspace. Recent advancements in ZSL have concentrated on enhancing the generalization ability of DNNs by incorporating identity-preserving constraints into the network.  These advancements typically utilize the network's latent features for classification or regression.  However, the performance of these methods is highly dependent on the quality of latent features, which are often produced by the network using class embeddings or attribute embeddings. By classifying M Es as robust, fragile, or critical, we reveal that the type of robust M E depends on the structure of the state space, specifically whether it is finite or infinite. When the state space is finite, the robust M E is stochastic, while it is deterministic when the state space is infinite.  The analysis also identifies conditions for strong and weak robustness in both finite and infinite state spaces. Furthermore, we determine the criteria for the existence of robust M Es and explore the structure of the set of robust M Es in the space of all M Es.  By demonstrating that this set is one-dimensional and consists of isolated points, we reveal the existence of a unique maximal and minimal element.  The study further confirms the existence of an infinite number of minimal elements and explains how to access them.  By examining the dynamics of these M Es, we identify and categorize their cyclic components, comutative components, and isomorphic components, ultimately revealing the vast diversity of robust M Es.  The analysis also implies that the set of weakly robust M Es is one-dimensional and consists of isolated points, along with a vast number of minimal elements, although these are yet to be fully identified.  The findings of this study open up new avenues for research by questioning whether the robust M Es with specific properties can be made weakly robust under particular transformations and whether the number of minimal elements for weak robustness can be exceeded.  The results of this study provide a theoretical framework for addressing these questions.  The research also identifies a connection between the existence of minimal M Es and the presence of minimal invariant subspaces in the space of stochastic matrices of a specific size, thereby contributing to both discrete-time evolution and the field of non-negative matrices.  The findings of this study provide a theoretical structure for the classification of M Es, which can be used to analyze real-world applications where the dynamics of M Es are observed numerically.  The results can help identify whether these applications involve robust, fragile, or critical M Es, thereby shedding light on their inherent properties.  The research also offers a method for numerically identifying the minimal M Es that give rise to these applications, which can contribute to understanding the dynamics of real-world systems.  The findings of this study can shed light on the behavior of reversible M Es with arbitrary state spaces, which has significant implications for both the theoretical and practical aspects of discrete-time evolution.

The researchers analyze this setup by examining various channel conditions and optimizing the power used by the user and relay to boost both the successful receipt rate and effective information transmission rate at the receiver. By comparing different channel scenarios, the researchers find that a two-channel relay transmission is most beneficial when there is no correlation between the user and receiver, as it offers the highest success receipt rate.   Conventional GNN models often have high inference costs due to their explicit
  neighborhood concepts, which can be difficult to activate efficiently. This
  presents a challenge for large-scale graph applications and makes them costly
  to implement in systems. A primary goal of this research is to develop a new
  family of GNN models that are both effective and have lower inference costs.
  The key contribution of this thesis is the introduction of a new GNN class
  called sample graph neural networks (SGNNs). These models utilize random neighbor
  concepts to capture neighborhood information and are based on the idea of
  selecting a subset of nodes as neighbors for each given node. This is in
  contrast to traditional GNNs that explicitly activate all neighbors of a given
  node.

  The research continues by investigating three key aspects of SGNNs. Firstly, it
  is demonstrated that SGNNs can achieve similar accuracy while reducing the
  inference cost. Secondly, a framework is proposed to evaluate the accuracy of
  SGNNs under different activation patterns. Finally, a comparative study is
  conducted to explore the differences between SGNNs and hard and soft GNNs under
  various activation schemes.

  The experimental results show that SGNNs can attain comparable accuracy while
  achieving a lower number of active nodes, which can lead to a lower overall
  inference cost. Additionally, the results indicate that SGNNs can provide more
  stable performance under different activation patterns. Ultimately, the
  empirical analysis supports the use of SGNNs for their efficient neighborhood

Our investigation focuses on multiple aspects: the semantic relationships between words, the overall meaning of a sentence, and the way phrases are interconnected. To uncover the recursive nature of language, we employ a range of supervised models, starting with a basic level and gradually increasing complexity. These models are based on the idea of combining individual word meanings through basic operations such as addition and multiplication. By introducing higher-level functions like exponentiation and modulo operations, as well as incorporating object-like entities, we develop more sophisticated mathematical structures. The higher-level models achieve comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art models in the space while significantly simplifying the underlying mathematical representations. Moreover, by leveraging the compositional structure of language, we demonstrate that certain complex phrases can be equivalently expressed using multiple, syntactically distinct forms. Our analysis reveals that lower-level distributional models are better equipped to capture the nuances of this equivalence. Additionally, we showcase that the recursive models are capable of accurately modeling entity-centric contexts, capturing a wide range of relationships between words, and understanding both basic and complex sentence structures. Ultimately, our results indicate that a systematic, mathematically defined language understanding framework can effectively learn and replicate the essential distributional properties of natural language, thereby validating the concept of compositional structure in Compositional Neural Networks. However, this is not the case for intuitionistic logic. There have been attempts to prove a completeness theorem for intuitionistic logic in a way that eliminates the reliance on ordering, but these attempts have failed. 

  In this paper, we show that there is no version of completeness for intuitionistic logic that relies only on algebraic principles. Our proof involves demonstrating the existence of a consistent algebraic version of intuitionistic logic with a finite number of axioms and rules, but no derivations that include every possible formula. This is an unusual consequence, as we would normally expect to be able to derive every possible formula in a consistent system.

This equivalence holds under the assumption that coefficients and decision variables at each stage are confined to convex polytopes and that a linear relationship exists between them. in semiconductor materials under photoexcitation is a well-known phenomenon with far-reaching implications in the analysis of optical properties. In organometallic compounds, the delocalization of charge carriers differs significantly from that within traditional inorganic semiconductors. Research has shown that these materials can exhibit a range of charged excitons. Our study focused specifically on the cobalt(II) tetrakis(acetoxy)phthalocyanine substance, an organometallic material, as it was recently identified as a semiconductor. Our investigation involved collecting reflection spectra in an oxygen atmosphere and applying theoretical simulations at low temperatures. These efforts yielded a comprehensive picture of the substance's electronic properties, revealing an intricate system comprised of multiple charged and neutral excitons. The scheduled infrared analysis scheduled to be carried out in this study was unfortunately cancelled due to the closure of our research facility due to the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result, we were able to simulate an IR spectrum and present it in this study instead, leading to the discovery of new charged and neutral excitons and bipolarons. Our research identified several key features, including the strongest absorption related to an allowed transition at 1.26 eV and the presence of multiple charged and neutral excitons and bipolarons. The discovery of these new features significantly expands the spectrum of electronic states in strong semiconductor materials. The findings of this study may also contribute to the discovery of new materials with diverse electronic properties and aid in the analysis of reflection and absorption spectra in strong semiconductors. In addition, a new method for calculating optical transitions using a spin-polarized version of the TDDFT technique was developed, allowing for a clearer distinction between various electronic transitions. Our research may lead to new insights in the field of organometallic materials and strong semiconductors, and new applications are also possible. Furthermore, the closure of our research facility due to the COVID-19 pandemic caused significant difficulties for young researchers, and in some cases, led to the cancellation of important studies, such as the research presented in this paper, significantly delaying their career development. To address this shortfall, a new paradigm, POMDP-IL, is introduced, which utilizes interactive learning to model the development of language.  In the POMDP-IL framework, language learners simultaneously discover both the intended meaning behind utterances and the rules governing language use.  A novel language model, called POMDP-IL-SAT, is developed to solve the POMDP-IL framework. While relation inference and property attribution tasks have been extensively explored, a relatively underinvestigated area is the semantic entailment relationship.  Entailment relationships are fundamental in understanding the nature of properties and the inference capabilities of knowledge graphs.  To address this gap, we introduce a new notion of semantic entailment, formulate it as a crowd-sourcing classification challenge, and conduct experiments on constructed knowledge graphs.  Our results indicate that the quality of properties and the consistency of knowledge graphs can be improved through the incorporation of semantic entailment information.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the value of semantic entailment in advancing property attribution and relation inference.  To facilitate future research, we provide publicly accessible knowledge graphs and crowd-sourcing classification data on entailment, properties, and inference.  Our research demonstrates that semantic entailment offers unique benefits in enhancing knowledge graphs, properties, and relations, and paves the way for new user-centered techniques. The results show that using a linear output in the decoder results in failure to recover the input data, while using a ReLU or sigmoid output leads to partial recovery. Conversely, using a linear input in the encoder results in partial recovery. Furthermore, the middle representation in these models does not exhibit the same characteristics as the input data. The research highlights the significant impact of linear layers in neural networks and the difficulty of recovering the original input data, a concept we call linear bias. The linear bias phenomenon is analyzed in more detail for autoencoders, and we observe that applying regularization to linear layers can improve partial recovery. The linear bias phenomenon also affects other types of neural networks, such as classifiers, and can be leveraged to create attacks on neural networks, a type of adversarial sample, as well as pseudo-labeled data. The research suggests potential methods for detecting linear bias and mitigating its effects, including changing the output layer parameterization, modifying the cost function, or using different network architectures. the prisoner's dilemma game, which has been extensively studied through evolutionary game theory.  The standard model assumes a randomly mixed population of players, but a more nuanced approach involves spatial structures, such as a grid where players are positioned close to one another.  Building upon this concept, a variant has been introduced in which players can only interact with the best players, effectively creating an 'elite challenge.'  Analyzing this model using computer simulations, researchers discovered that a key threshold exists at which cooperation emerges and dominates the population, and this occurs through a mechanism of cooperative spread among neighboring players, even without any mutual cooperation occurring initially.  The presence of an incentive to interact with the elite players forces the standard players to engage in cooperative behavior, and as a result, a network of connected, cooperative agents develops.  Interestingly, this model has real-world parallels in economics and politics, where groups, such as corporations and political parties, can be considered as homogeneous, cooperative populations seeking to outdo their competitive counterparts.  The novel social dilemma presented here offers a unique opportunity for further theoretical and experimental investigation.

  The processing of medical images plays a vital role in diagnosing and treating diseases. However, certain problems in data acquisition can result in biased images. For instance, diseases may appear more pronounced in images taken during peak seasons or those affecting a specific gender. Furthermore, issues in data acquisition may result in incomplete or unrepresentative information in spatial, temporal, or channel contexts. 

  Various forms of compensation for such problems have been explored. Initially, techniques involving data augmentation, classification balancing, image standardization, and information matching were employed. Later, more advanced approaches including probabilistic models, optimization-based methods, and deep learning techniques involving loss function modifications and immune algorithms were developed. 

  Each of these methods presents unique challenges. For instance, data augmentation may not be sufficient to address problems in data acquisition. Furthermore, standardization may not effectively represent the underlying variations in different modalities, and high-performant algorithms may not effectively address problems in data acquisition or presentation. 

  Addressing these problems has various implications on medical image analysis tasks. For instance, techniques involving data augmentation may not effectively address problems in data acquisition in multiple contexts. However, deep learning algorithms showing robustness in different acquisition contexts may require expertise in information acquisition. 

  Ultimately, compensation for problems in medical image analysis is a never-ending pursuit due to the diverse problems in data acquisition in the medical sector. Nevertheless, we hope this review provides a thorough understanding of the problems in medical image analysis, along with potential techniques and methods for addressing these problems, and encourages researchers to continue working in this area. This research explores how native English speakers use 'like' to imply opposition by analyzing comparisons involving objects that aren't inherently opposite but are commonly seen as such (e.g., dogs and cats). One key challenge in GAN development involves achieving stable training, since traditional approaches using supervised feedback can result in model instability. To address this issue, researchers have explored the use of self-monitoring GANs, which allow models to automatically assess their own performance. However, detecting training instability remains difficult in these models, causing them to cease training prematurely. To resolve this problem, we present a novel method using a trust metric to support the training of GANs. Our approach employs a network to calculate a trust metric for each generator based on its divergence from the target distribution, calculated via the Kane-Strassen statistic. During training, generators with low trust scores are prioritised, receiving more updates to accelerate convergence. Our experiments demonstrate that this method allows GANs to complete training on challenging datasets such as ImageNet, producing higher-resolution results compared to existing self-monitoring GANs. Additionally, we provide detailed analysis and visual examples of our model, outlining future research directions. Our code and model will be publicly available, enabling further research into this topic. Our first method significantly enhances the previous distance approximation technique by reducing the error to $O(\log n)$ when the metric is $\delta$-thin. Consequently, we derive a new online algorithm with an $O(\log n)$-time approximation ratio for reaching the optimal shortest path. Our second approach involves constructing a new shortest path using only a subset of the metric points, where the error is limited to an $O(\log^2 n)$ approximation ratio. Furthermore, we derive a new online algorithm with an $O(\log^2 n)$-time approximation ratio for reaching the optimal shortest path. Notably, these results generalize previous findings for the static metric problem. Additionally, we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for the distance approximation problem, where the metric undergoes $\Omega(\log n)$ consecutive changes. Our study also introduces a new technique for "charging" the shortest path, which enables efficient verification of the distance approximation ratio. Furthermore, we investigate the time complexity of constructing an exact shortest path in an online metric with a fixed set of points, where the metric undergoes dynamic changes after each point is added. Our results indicate that this problem is computationally intractable, with a time complexity of $\Omega(n^2)$ for the time required to approximate the shortest path. To resolve this, we attempt to group the metric points into $k$ sets and then calculate the shortest path in each group. have become a preferred method for zero-shot learning (ZSL), which enables the classification of novel categories without using any samples from those categories.  Recent advancements in ZSL have concentrated on enhancing the generalization ability of DNNs by incorporating identity-preserving constraints into the network.  These advancements typically utilize the network's latent features for classification or regression.  However, the performance of these methods is highly dependent on the quality of latent features, which are often produced by the network using class embeddings or attribute embeddings.  Notably, the performance of these methods deteriorates when the embeddings used are of low quality.  In an effort to enhance the generalization ability of DNNs for ZSL, we propose a novel method that trains the network to preserve identity-independent constraints.  By doing so, we achieve robust latent features that can withstand variations in class embeddings or attribute embeddings.  We evaluate the robustness of our method, dubbed IIC-ConDRO, by analyzing its generalization ability when the network's latent features are used for both classification and regression tasks.  In our experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of IIC-ConDRO by comparing it to existing methods on the social media datasets AWESOME-cats and cats-vs-dogs.  We also validate the robustness of IIC-ConDRO by conducting an analysis that involves manipulating the network's latent features.  Ultimately, the results of our analysis demonstrate the efficacy of IIC-ConDRO for ZSL.  The code for IIC-ConDRO is available at https://github.com/indigo2/tree-sde-zsl-conditional-dropout. In this research, we investigate the utility of two novel constraint relaxation techniques - Sentence Anchoring and Most Probable Solution - aiming to identify at least one optimal solution in polynomial time for certain combinatorial optimization problems. Furthermore, we observed significant improvements in obtaining optimal solutions for approximately 75% of combinatorial optimization challenges in comparison to traditional optimization techniques. However, the results indicated a pronounced decrease in efficiency for some challenges. Ultimately, the outcome of each constraint relaxation technique proved unpredictable and dependent on the problem at hand - suggesting the integration of these methods as versatile tools in a comprehensive optimization toolkit. In fact, the experiments indicated distinct differences in behavior and performance between these two constraint relaxation techniques. Through empirical analysis, we found a notable correlation between the effectiveness of each constraint relaxation technique and the number of feasible solutions in the global solution landscape. By comparing five approaches to dispatching drones for emergency responses - a stochastic method involving chance-constrained programming, a method using linear programming, a method using non-linear programming, a method simulating the drones' flight, and a method using a mathematical optimization problem with linear constraints - researchers evaluated and contrasted their effectiveness and efficiency.  Analysis revealed that the dispatch methods studied had differing levels of efficiency in terms of the time it took for each drone to arrive at the emergency, with the most efficient method, the mathematical optimization approach, taking 92 seconds to dispatch drones versus 248 seconds for the second-best method. Furthermore, the problem of dispatching drones for emergency responses is a complex problem, and there may be other issues to consider, so it is not a straightforward solution, and more research is needed.   The novel quark composition, denoted as $Q$, with a mass higher than the nucleon, 
  can be conceptualized as a linear superposition of its quark components $uqs$ and $uds$. 
  Given its large mass, $Q$ predominantly undergoes hadronic decay into three leptons. 
  We derive strict limitations from dimensional analysis on the coupling constants involved 
  in the decay processes $Q\to \pi\pi\nu_\tau$, $Q\to K\gamma$, $Q\to \pi\gamma$, 
  $Q\to K_\mathrm{long}S$ and $Q\to KS$, and investigate two theoretical models, 
  $\mathrm{SU}(3)_\mathrm{Q}$
  allowing for the diagonalization of the quark mass matrix and 
  $\mathrm{U}(1)_\mathrm{EM}$
  incorporating electromagnetic interactions to derive bounds on the nucleon decay into pion pairs. 
  We also examine the constraints imposed by the discrete symmetries $\mathrm{CP}$, $\mathrm{T}$, 
  $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{CPT}$ and $\mathrm{PT}$, 
  and evaluate the feasibility of searching for the new baryon $Q$ using neutrino experiments. 
  Our analysis also includes an examination of the constraints on the vector-like vector quark model. 
  Finally, our investigation into nucleon decay into meson pairs leads to a comprehensive set of bounds. 
  We calculate the nucleon decay into electron-meson correlation functions, 
  and derive limits on nucleon decay into pion pairs by incorporating the pion form factor and 
  leveraging data from pi-zero production. 
  Our study yields strict limitations at low momentum transfers, 
  Tranquility bounds in medium momentum transfers, and Warick bounds at high momentum transfers.

By analyzing these lines, scientists have found that the velocity distribution of the gas is much narrower than expected. Developing a mathematical model for this phenomenon, researchers have found that the distribution can be explained by a normal probability density function with a mean of $6.8 \, \mathrm{km/s}$ and a standard deviation of $\sqrt{95}/6.8 \, \mathrm{km/s}$. However, this model fails to account for anomalies observed at high velocities, leading to a poorer fit at those speeds. An alternative model based on a combination of a normal probability density function and a Cauchy distribution is also considered. Although both models provide a satisfactory explanation for the observed velocity distribution, anomalies at high velocities cannot be accounted for by a single velocity distribution. Furthermore, these models assume that the mass of the galactic halo is composed of a single, uniform particle, making it difficult to reconcile with small particle masses predicted by certain theories, such as the behavior of pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone bosons. An analysis of the galactic halo velocity distribution has also been carried out using data from the Hubble Space Telescope. In this case, a Cauchy distribution is found to provide a better fit than a normal probability density function. An algorithm for accurately measuring the galactic halo velocity distribution has also been developed. This algorithm relies on a robust method based on a statistical analysis of data from multiple observations and is found to provide reliable results even when dealing with incomplete or irregularly spaced data. An analysis using this algorithm of several commonly cited models for the galactic halo velocity distribution confirms the findings of the previous study. Finally, an analysis using a combination of this algorithm and data from the Hubble Space Telescope has shown that the velocity distribution can be accounted for by a single velocity distribution, provided the average mass of the galactic halo is much less than the mass of the sun. Such issues could lead to a phenomenon known as indirect bias, where the output of one AI system influences the input of another, potentially exacerbating initial errors or prejudices. In essence, indirect bias poses a challenge to fair AI outcomes, particularly in scenarios where users' preferences vary based on classification results. In such cases, simply addressing direct prejudice may not be sufficient; instead, further investigation is required to identify and rectify indirect prejudices as well. In this research, we introduce a solution to detect and eliminate indirect prejudices within a common classification task. Our approach links the problem of detecting indirect prejudices to the identification of augmenting graphs in hypergraph systems and suggests a metric for measuring the presence of indirect prejudices. Furthermore, we outline a method for rectifying the prejudices, making our solution applicable to a wide range of hypergraph systems, including scenarios where the initial data is partially missing. Our solution is further validated through the testing of a constructed dataset. Therefore, a new model, StrongStrongBaselines, is introduced which combines the multi-scale matrix-based matching cost of Strong-LoSAs with the robust ranking loss function of the strong baseline model, eliminating the need for a two-stage post-processing pipeline in AnoBaselines. Typically, individual events are classified into basic categories or weights assigned to them, then grouped into more detailed subcategories based on consistent patterns in the first step. However, commonly used techniques rely solely on the correlation of a single set of data, overlooking the multi-dimensional relationships present in other datasets associated with the event. Each event's characteristics can include multiple datasets collected at different times, such as spectral patterns, light curves, and time-of-arrival data, which often provide independent insights into the event. Despite this, existing techniques have focused solely on the correlation of one dataset. This paper presents a new method, Multivariate Weighted Cluster Analysis (MWCA), designed to account for the complexity of multi-dimensional datasets, even when they have been transformed into a single feature space. MWCA incorporates techniques such as PCA, dimensionality expansion, and weighted clustering to provide a comprehensive understanding of the events, even when they have significant anisotropic correlations. The utility of MWCA is illustrated using synthetic datasets with varying levels of anisotropy, before being applied to four real-world datasets associated with gamma-ray bursts. MWCA's results are contrasted with those of traditional techniques, showing MWCA identifies more precise patterns and incorporates more information from the data, including correlations and higher-dimensional relationships. The code for MWCA is openly available on GitHub at the address: https://github.com/shawn-k-keenan/MWCA. generalized Lorentz-buckling mechanical models (GBM) often employ overly simplistic representations of material anisotropy. In an effort to improve this, a new expression for linearized anisotropic force fields is proposed, drawing on the fully linearized GBM. This new approach is demonstrated to offer a well-defined, unambiguous method for importing anisotropic behavior into FF representations. Various ways in which this model can be used to model common types of anisotropy are detailed, along with a general algorithm for converting GBM parameters to force field parameters and vice versa. Several numerical examples are provided to illustrate the success of this methodology in capturing anisotropic effects within FFs. One of the case studies, in particular, focuses on the modeling of wood's unique forms of anisotropy. This research opens up the possibility of incorporating sophisticated anisotropic behavior into classical force fields, thereby enhancing their utility in simulations of anisotropic materials. Force fields based on linearized GBM can also serve as a starting point for the development of more accurate GBMs that take into account non-linear strain measures. This, in turn, could enable simulations in which anisotropic behavior is highly strain-dependent. Lastly, it is essential to note that this new approach to FFs will inevitably result in a rise in the required precomputational resources. As such, it is crucial to utilize high-performance computational methods, such as those offered by supercomputing centers, in order to successfully implement these enhanced FFs. This research is an urgent requirement, given the ever-growing availability of computational power and the ever-expanding importance of anisotropic materials in industry and science. In light of this, it is not unreasonable to anticipate that this methodology will be further developed to account for other factors, such as variable density, once more efficient computational resources become available.

This concept has significant potential to accelerate training, particularly when tailored to accommodate instruction-level parallelism found in standard CPU architectures. So far, numerous studies focus on training models using general purpose instructions, overlooking the inherent multi Instruction Level Parallelism (ILP) capabilities these architectures provide. By contrast with the standard IllustrisT simulation that assumes a uniform rate of star formation, our model predicts a faster early increase in the number of supermassive black holes within the first billion years by taking into account the impact of intense UV radiation from the first generation of stars on gas within the first generation of galaxies. Additionally, we find that at higher redshifts ($z>5$) the rate of supermassive black hole formation is significantly enhanced under conditions of higher gas pressures, as simulated by the simulation. By the time galaxies reach their current sizes, this pressure effect is largely overpowered by the impact of star formation on gas within galaxies, resulting in a relatively slow increase in the number of supermassive black holes at higher redshifts. This study focuses on a specific type of outliers present in datasets, specifically those in the form of data points that adhere to a linear relationship, known as linear anomalies.  Linear anomalies can be thought of as points that disrupt the underlying linear relationship among the data, and their detection is crucial for ensuring the reliability of machine learning models.  Although previous studies have addressed linear anomalies, they often rely on assumptions that don't hold true in real-world scenarios, such as knowing the linear relationship among the data or being able to visualize the data.  As a result, this study proposes a novel approach to linear anomaly detection, specifically designed for cases where the nature of the linear relationship is unknown.  Our approach is based on an analysis of directed graphs and is tested on artificially created data, as well as on data from actual applications, to showcase its effectiveness and robustness.  Importantly, our approach does not require any pre-existing knowledge of the linear relationship, and it offers a clear explanation of the detected linear anomalies.  Furthermore, our approach can detect multiple linear anomalies present in each data point, and it has been released as an open-source tool that can be used to detect linear anomalies in various types of data.  This study demonstrates that the nature of linear anomalies can change significantly depending on the data at hand, and it provides a detailed classification of linear anomalies, specifically in the context of multivariate data.  Interestingly, our approach was found to accurately detect linear anomalies in image data, and it was successfully used to detect linear anomalies in data related to real-estate values and law studies. Throughout the decades, it has been explored through multiple methods including stress-strain cycles, creep and creep-recovery tests, and oscillatory shear measurements. Owing to its significance, it is essential to be able to accurately analyze data obtained from these experiments. However, extracting relevant information from these tests can be challenging, especially when the resulting data cannot be described by a single simple model due to the underlying complexity of the viscoelastic material. This complexity is particularly evident during stress-relaxation experiments where the material's response cannot be explained by a single exponential function. As a result, various techniques such as the Maxwell model, the Maxwell-Voigert model, the Kelvin model, the Maxwell-Kelvin model, the "bag-of-branches" model, the "branching factor method", and the Cole-Diepenbrock model are employed to analyze stress-relaxation data. 

  In this work, a detailed comparison of the aforementioned models is presented along with the extraction of key parameters. Although previous studies have utilized these models, they often lack detailed comparisons of the obtained results. Moreover, our study expands on the analysis by the Cole-Diepenbrock team, taking the discussion a step further while providing a comprehensive overview of the strengths and limitations of the examined models. This study also highlights a often-overlooked aspect - the uncertainty associated with the obtained parameters. Furthermore, in addition to comparing the models, we also explore the feasibility of constructing a tree-like representation of the material's relaxation functions. This study demonstrates that accurate fitting of stress-relaxation data using the Cole-Diepenbrock model supports the generation of such a representation, allowing the visualization of the material's relaxation function. This novel approach offers a straightforward, intuitive way to understand the material's composition and its relaxation processes. This study provides a detailed overview of the examined models, offering insights for researchers working in this domain.

This requirement is a significant improvement over the constraints typically associated with the Cole-Diepenbrock method, which demands a specific material history. This flexibility makes the method more versatile and accessible.

The traditional model, used extensively in non-stochastic and stochastic studies, divides individuals into two compartments: the compartment of infectious individuals and the compartment of the rest. The proposed model, applicable to both individual-based and continuum type epidemic simulations, includes an additional compartment: susceptible individuals currently being infected. The proposed model can be extended by adding a compartment for individuals in pre-symptomatic periods, useful particularly in simulations of individual-based models. The main goal of introducing this additional compartment is to reflect the fact that infectious individuals have not yet produced infectious particles. The model can be evaluated by comparing the average durations of symptoms and latency, as well as the relative rates of infection occurring between an infectious individual and a susceptible individual, and between two infectious individuals. The model is particularly relevant to the COVID-19 pandemic, as research has shown that there is a significant difference between these two relative rates, and this difference may contribute substantially to the epidemic spread. While the thermal production of axions has been extensively studied, particularly in the context of QCD, the production of these particles via the decay of cosmic strings has not received the same level of attention.
