proportion of infected individuals exhibit no symptoms. Traditional epidemic models
are often based on the assumption that social distancing measures primarily affect
symptomatic users, but in reality, they may also impact asymptomatic users.
This study considers a basic SIS model, where social distancing is assumed to apply
equally to both symptomatic and asymptomatic users. We develop a dynamic model
that describes how social distancing interventions impact the spread of epidemics
and discuss its long-term behavior. Specifically, the model reveals that if a
significant portion of the population engages in social distancing, the epidemic
can be avertible, regardless of the extent to which asymptomatic users practice
social distancing. Conversely, if social distancing interventions fail to reach a
critical threshold of the population, the epidemic will inevitably spread
unrestricted. Notably, the model shows that social distancing interventions can
reduce the peak incidence of epidemics, but will have no effect if a sufficient
proportion of the population practices social distancing regardless of whether
they exhibit symptoms or not. If a limited proportion of the population
practices social distancing even in the presence of symptoms, the epidemic can
still be avertable, but will peak at a higher rate without them. Ultimately, the
model highlights the crucial role of social distancing interventions in avertive
efforts targeting individuals who exhibit no symptoms. The non-symptomatic
population's responses to these interventions differ fundamentally from those of
the symptomatic population, but are essential for collaborative epidemic
interventions. We further analyze the model's predictive power by testing it
using real-world data from Chengdu, China, in the early stages of the Covid-19
outbreak. The results from this application confirm the model's accuracy and
predictive power. The model suggests implementing targeted interventions at
critical points in the epidemic where asymptomatic cases increase significantly,
such as school closures or the cancellation of mass public events. These findings
are valuable for understanding and managing the Covid-19 epidemic as well as
potential future epidemics caused by coronavirus variants. The model is
generalizable to various types of viruses, but requires regular updates of the
estimated transmission coefficients to remain effective against dynamic epidemics.

A well-established technique for achieving personalized recommendations is collaborative filtering, which it involves identifying similar behavior patterns in user data to generate recommendations.  We investigate the feasibility of integrating collaborative filtering with relational databases to support the rapid development and deployment of recommender systems.  Our research highlights the technical difficulties that arise when attempting to integrate these concepts and proposes an in-place table-based approach to facilitate the development of such systems.  This approach utilizes user ID, item ID, and behavior quantity columns to store relevant data, allowing for efficient and effective recommendations to be generated.  We evaluate our method by applying it to several publicly available datasets and compare the results to those obtained from traditional signature-based collaborative filtering techniques.  The evaluation reveals that our table-based approach is a viable and efficient method for achieving personal recommendations.  Consequently, this approach can be readily incorporated into database management systems to serve online recommendations.  As an example, our technique is demonstrated in an Oracle database environment to generate movie recommendations.  The results demonstrate the accuracy of the recommendations generated using our table-based method to be on par with those obtained from signature-based collaborative filtering.  Additionally, the time required to run the recommendations was found to be significantly faster, amounting to a 2 to 3 order of magnitude improvement.  Furthermore, the integration of our table-based method with database management systems enables the capabilities of transaction management, data recovery, and data locking, thereby significantly enhancing the robustness of the recommender system.  In contrast, the signature-based collaborative filtering technique is notable for its lack of these database management system features.  In summary, the value of our contribution is multi-faceted. This study investigates the effects of targeted interventions, such as vaccinations, on a network-associated dynamical system. The existence of an optimal control strategy is proven to mitigate disease spread in a highly connected network, specifically the Watts-Strogatz network, by inducing a local damage with minimal disruption to global network structure. on certain semantic segmentation tasks, they often generate overly smooth, artificial images. Real-world images can exhibit imperfections such as texture, shadows, and reflections that may mislead these models and extend their incorrectly applied segmentation patterns to other settings. Our goal is to develop a novel approach to enhance the robustness and generalizability of deep segmentation networks. We propose a new task called edge-alpha manipulation, where an incomplete edge map and texture-like alpha channel are provided alongside the RGB image, allowing the model to predict incomplete edge maps and complete alpha channels. This hybrid input facilitates the transmission of coarse-scale low-frequency details to the edge map and high-frequency details to the alpha channel. Consequently, the model can integrate high-frequency details into segmentation edges, yielding more natural and realistic segmentation boundaries. We evaluate our method on various segmentation datasets and observe considerable improvements in both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Notably, edge-alpha manipulation demonstrates enhanced robustness against artificial segmentation boundaries, as well as segmentation networks trained with synthetic data featuring artificial textures, shadows, and reflections. Additionally, our method can filter out artificial textures from segmentation boundaries, making it an indispensable tool for numerous downstream tasks where natural edge maps are essential, such as 3D surface reconstruction and key-point detection. We anticipate that our approach will serve as a building block for developing more robust and generalizable deep segmentation networks. The source code and manipulated edge maps and alpha channels can be accessed at https://github.com/ghleebed/EarMan++. We introduce a distinct perspective on (finite) measures that enables the reapplication of the Krein-Smulyan theorem, thus establishing the representation theorem in a more general context.  This proof relies on a fixed point theorem tailored to ordered complete chains, which we establish as a new concept.  We also explore the related fixed point theorem for ordered Tychonoff spaces and derive representations for finite positive measures on spaces without upper bounds and countable spaces without a least element. Our proof of the fundamental theorem of finite measures also yields a new proof of the Radon-Nikodym derivative theorem.  We demonstrate the necessity and sufficiency of the key derivative theorem condition using a specific measure that assigns 1 to sets containing the least element of an ordered space. We also show that the fundamental theorem of finite measures implies the existence of Haar measures for certain spaces with invariant groups.  Specifically, these groups can be replaced by countable groups in Tychonoff spaces or groups of finite cardinality in spaces without upper bounds.  Furthermore, these results generalize the existing theories of measures on spaces with invariant groups, particularly for the groups $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$.  We also note that the fundamental theorem of finite measures is equivalent to the existence of Haar measures for countable groups.
